data_pipeline:
ONE script, `code/build/bake.py`, run with /opt/anaconda3/envs/bio/bin/python. It holds every absolute input path; everything it writes is relative and relocatable. Idempotent, resumable per stage, and it fails loudly on any assertion rather than silently shifting data. Total runtime dominated by the optional STREME gap-fill.

STAGE 0 — PREFLIGHT ASSERTIONS (~5 s). Re-runs the coordinate contract over all 889,215 rows: `seq[motif_start : motif_end + 1] == motifs` must hold for 889,215/889,215 and `motif_length == motif_end - motif_start + 1` for 100%. Re-runs the annotation-coverage check that reproduces all 8 published percentages under the `applies` field of annotation_coverage_stats.json. Both are regression tests: a future data refresh that changes the convention fails the build instead of shifting every highlight by one base.

STAGE 1 — DUCKDB CORE (measured 2.4 s, output 225.5 MB). From motif_full_annotations.parquet (889,215 x 24) and GRCh37_latest_rna_sequence_pairs_long_transcript.parquet:
  - `motif` (889,215 rows): typed down to INTEGER/REAL/SMALLINT, protein-layer annotation columns wrapped in `CASE WHEN region='protein'` — this fixes the 209,959 spurious MobiDB, 1,825 IDPO and 665 SignalP rows on UTR motifs. Verified post-build: 0 rows where region<>'protein' AND mobidb IS NOT NULL.
  - `tx` (19,210 rows): `SELECT DISTINCT ON (refseq_id_without_ver)` collapses the 21,667 source rows losslessly (all 1,296 duplicate groups byte-identical).
  - `gene_cluster` (541,746 rows): DISTINCT (sequence_id, gene_symbol, cluster, region) — the co-occurrence workhorse.
  - Indexes on motif(gene_symbol), motif(cluster), motif(sequence_id), gene_cluster(cluster), gene_cluster(sequence_id), tx(sequence_id).

STAGE 2 — ID-BEARING ANNOTATION REBUILD (~5 min). The five comma-joined string columns in the master table are NOT parsed — comma-splitting is wrong for 41.34% of annotated protein motifs on InterPro and 6.89% on UniProt. Instead, re-joined on raw_motif_index: `interpro_acc` from processed/01.interpro/motif_interpro_annotations.parquet column overlapping_interpro_labels (15,216 distinct IPRs) + interpro_entry_map.csv (ipr, name, type, go_ids, go_names); `uniprot_feat` recomputed from processed/03.uniprot/uniprot_annotation.parquet (1,577,512 features, 35 types) keeping type + start + end, with empty-description structural features labelled by type rather than dropped (~756k hits over 231,439 motifs, ~2 min); `idpo_id` from processed/05.idpo/motif_idpo_annotations.parquet column idpo_ids; `elm_id` re-joined from raw_annotations/02.elm/elm_instances.tsv + elm_classes.tsv; `uniprot_acc` from data/idmapping_2026_05_08.tsv (16,911 of 18,093 transcripts). Original joined strings are kept as `*_legacy_string` for provenance but never rendered as chips.

STAGE 3 — SUPPORTING TABLES. Loaded into the same DuckDB file: pairs (protein_utr_FINAL_scores.csv, 180,000 x 15), edges (phylo_corrected_candidates.csv, 2,620), enrichment (cluster_term_enrichment.csv.gz, 260,572 x 18, de-duplicated on (cluster, source, display) keeping min fdr_cluster to kill the 17,056 duplicated display groups), consensus_meta (1,226), consensus_pairs (consensus_pair_scores.csv.gz, 49,547 x 22), modules (modules.json expanded to a flat 513-row cluster->module map), module_go (6,389), module_genes (12,345), go_specificity (42), raw_top30 (30), domains (annotated_protein_sequences.csv, 109,110), rbp_peaks (motif_rbp_overlaps.parquet, 2,671,559), genome_map (motif_genome_mappings_grch37.parquet, 634,749), and the validation tables (m1_m2_rbp_enrichment 185, m1_m2_apex_localization 9, motif_2x2_kinetics_summary, ribomap_validation 859, tls_nuclear_degradation_M5 206).

STAGE 4 — DERIVED ARTIFACTS THAT EXIST NOWHERE ON DISK. (a) `meta_edges` — the 6x6 module adjacency, four lines of pandas, values M1-M2 244, M1-M5 192, M2-M3 167, M1-M6 32, M1-M3 30, M2-M5 28, M3-M4 22, M5-M6 15, then a tail to 1. (b) `layout.json` — d3-force run once over the 519-node/2,620-edge graph with per-module centroid attractors and a protein-left/UTR-right constraint, module block order from node_select.order_modules(). (c) `cluster_position` — 20-bin relative-position histograms for all 900 clusters (84 KB), validated against the 142 clusters in streme_pos_cache_all6.pkl. (d) `cluster_name` — the three-tier display name (37 curated / 463 top-FDR-term / 437 synthesized). (e) `availability` — the per-transcript panel manifest. (f) `excluded_transcripts` — the 1,117 motif-free RefSeq ids with the reason, 666 of them 'transcript length exceeds the 7,784 nt model context'. (g) `carrier_tier` — the tier A / literal / fuzzy-carrier classification generalized from find_m4_examples.py across all six modules.

STAGE 5 — PWM BUNDLE + OPTIONAL STREME GAP-FILL. consensus_repertoire.pkl (513 clusters, 451 with a significant motif, 1,226 motifs, 56,808 cells) is rounded to 4 dp and written as `pwm.json` (~0.56 MB). Optionally, `--fill-streme` runs the existing pipeline on the 387 never-run clusters using windows_fasta() and run_streme() from 16_consensus_repertoire.py verbatim, so new matrices are method-identical to the 513 on disk. Survey [clusters] measured 64.3 s for a protein cluster and 5-10 s for a UTR cluster, ~2.4 CPU-hours single-threaded or ~15 min at WORKERS=10; I did not re-verify this. ~100-150 protein clusters are expected to still return nothing significant.

STAGE 6 — NTSCORE. The two HDF5 caches are copied verbatim into the snapshot, not transformed: data/outputs_utr3_score_0318.h5 (169.5 MB, 18,585 groups) and explore_biology/01.protein_localization/analysis/data/h5cache/outputs_utr5_score_0326.h5 (118.5 MB, 18,093 groups). Copying rather than repacking is deliberate — random group access is already 0.20-0.29 ms and the arrays are verified 1:1 with region length. The bake asserts key coverage against the motif transcript set and records the utr3/utr5 key-count mismatch (18,585 vs 18,093) in the manifest.

STAGE 7 — UMAP SNAPSHOT. cca_winner_umap.npy (180000 x 2 float32) and row_index.csv are copied from the v3 analysis tree with their source path and mtime recorded, because nothing in the v4 pipeline regenerates them and the directory could be cleaned up without warning. Quantized to uint16 xy over the bounding box (max error 0.000234 data units) plus uint16 npmi and uint8 module channels, ~0.99 MB gzipped.

STAGE 8 — MANIFEST + STATIC EXPORT. `manifest.json` records the absolute source path, byte size, mtime and SHA-256 of every input, plus a semver snapshot version and build timestamp. `--emit-static` then walks the read-only route handlers offline and writes their JSON responses into a directory tree mirroring the API paths, producing the archival fallback bundle.

OUTPUT SIZES: portal.duckdb 225.5 MB (measured) + ntscore_utr3.h5 169.5 MB + ntscore_utr5.h5 118.5 MB + pwm.json 0.56 MB + layout/meta/manifest ~1 MB = ~515 MB total, baked into the Docker image as an immutable layer. The static export adds ~110 MB.

phases.name: P0 — Data foundation, API skeleton, and the deploy path
phases.deliverable: bake.py stages 0-4 and 8 producing portal.duckdb plus the manifest; a FastAPI app with the meta, search, transcript, cluster, module, network and edge read endpoints returning pydantic-typed JSON; the AST compiler with its guardrails and both /query endpoints; a Dockerfile with data baked in; the container running on Cloud Run behind the real hostname with /healthz green; CI that runs the preflight assertions.
phases.exit_criteria: The preflight assertions pass on all 889,215 rows and reproduce all 8 published coverage percentages. `SELECT count(*) FROM motif WHERE region<>'protein' AND mobidb IS NOT NULL` returns 0. Every endpoint returns a validated response under 100 ms p95 against a local load of 20 concurrent clients. The container is reachable at the production URL and a `docker run` from the published image serves the same responses. No front-end work has started.

phases.name: P1 — R1: the transcript view
phases.deliverable: The full gene page: aligned region tracks, the NTScore line track from HDF5, the windowed monospace sequence pane, the single-lane motif span layer, ruler and minimap, pLDDT and InterPro and UniProt and RBP and miRNA lanes, the motif inspector with source-badged annotation chips, the virtualized motif table, filter chips, the availability manifest, all three empty-state cards, and CSV/FASTA/BED export.
phases.exit_criteria: ACTB (NM_001101) renders exactly 3 5'UTR, 13 3'UTR and 4 protein motifs, all three 5'UTR motifs in utr5_0004, and TIAL1 annotated on the 45-nt AU-rich 3'UTR element — the one-glance validation of coordinates, join, clustering and annotations. Searching TTN returns the explained exclusion, not a blank. NM_001267550 (no motifs) and a transcript missing a region both render their explanatory card. The 7,601-nt worst-case 3'UTR pans at 60 fps. No UTR panel displays a protein-disorder term.

phases.name: P2 — R2: the cluster view
phases.deliverable: The region-variant cluster page: SVG logo renderer over the PWM bundle, consensus list with coverage bars, positional histogram, enrichment dot plot with contingency tooltips, the instance-frequency fallback, the two-tier partner table with expandable protein features and gate gauges, size/score/pLDDT/composition panels, instance and carrier tables, the three-tier auto-name badge and the logo provenance badge.
phases.exit_criteria: utr5_0096 and utr3_0215 reproduce the hand-checked numbers in m4_motif_examples/README.md (AGCAGA coverage 0.253/70 carriers; UCAUC 0.150/64; UCUCC 0.511/155). utr3_0463 shows SLBP at fold 48.6 (k=22, n=196). A cluster with zero FDR<0.05 terms (utr5_0090) shows greyed non-significant rows plus the instance-frequency fallback, never a blank tab. A cluster with no PWM shows the top-k-mer table and says why. No cluster renders as a bare id.

phases.name: P3 — R3: the network and module views
phases.deliverable: All three network scopes (meta 6-node, full 519-node, per-module) on the frozen build-time layout with a live-force toggle; node and edge drawers with the tiered consensus panel, gate gauges and live-computed carrier lists; the score slider with live counts; the cross-module toggle and meta-adjacency heatmap; the persistent caveat bar; the six module pages with GO dot plot, trusted toggle, specificity slope, member gene table and the module-specific validation panels.
phases.exit_criteria: The full graph draws as one connected component of 513 nodes plus the three isolated dyads, with all 757 cross-module edges present and toggleable. Clicking prot_0040 x utr5_0004 shows score 1.7694, co_count 175, 23 clades, ZNF 0.000, both consensus logos, and 173 carrier genes computed in under 20 ms. A cross-module edge shows the tier-2 'consensus per cluster' fallback with its tier named. The M5 page shows all seven kinetics metrics including the four non-significant ones, and the M1/M2 APEX panel shows lamina q=0.725 and OMM q=0.551 rather than omitting them.

phases.name: P4 — The analytical workbench and pair explorer
phases.deliverable: The AST builder with per-leaf cardinality and cost estimation, the UpSet intersection plot, the result table, the on-the-fly enrichment panel with vocabulary and universe selectors, the SQL preview, permalinks and saved queries; the canvas UMAP with brush/lasso, the NPMI histogram with draggable threshold, the raw-vs-corrected artifact scatter, and the pair table.
phases.exit_criteria: A three-term query (utr5_0079 AND prot_0072 AND NOT ELAVL1) returns in under 50 ms with a correct UpSet decomposition, and a two-term co-occurrence returns the 51 transcripts / 173 genes that match the precomputed files. Enrichment over utr3_0463's carriers returns SLBP at the top with its universe named and the deviation from the published gene-level number explained in the panel. The 180,000-point scatter pans and brushes at 60 fps. Every guardrail (depth, term count, timeout, row cap) is exercised by a test and surfaces as UI rather than a 500.

phases.name: P5 — Provenance, hardening, and the survival plan
phases.deliverable: The methods and caveats view with the verdict table, Meff bars, deflation chart, funnel, gate cards, coverage bars, verbatim quotes, snapshot manifest, download catalog and live OpenAPI browser; the `--emit-static` fallback bundle published to GitHub Pages under the lab org; the Zenodo deposit of the DuckDB file plus the Docker image digest; uptime monitoring; rate limiting and request logging; accessibility and dark-mode passes.
phases.exit_criteria: The paper can cite a Zenodo DOI, a container digest and a live URL, and the portal still works if any one of the three disappears. `docker run <digest>` on a clean machine reproduces the site offline. The static fallback serves R1/R2/R3 read paths with the workbench and NTScore explicitly marked unavailable. Every module and edge view carries the co-occurrence caveat, and every enrichment number is traceable to a k/n/K/N tooltip. Uptime monitoring alerts a shared institutional address, not a personal one.

tradeoffs:
THE CENTRAL TENSION, STATED HONESTLY. Survey [scale] measured a static per-gene shard answering R1 in 1.13 ms against 179 ms for pyarrow filtering, and recommended a fully static site. That recommendation is correct for R1 alone. It is wrong for this brief, and the measurements above show why: a static build cannot serve the 288 MB of NTScore HDF5, cannot answer a boolean query over 541,746 gene×cluster memberships that the user composes at runtime, and cannot run enrichment against a gene set that does not exist until someone builds it. My own benchmark of the DuckDB path found the gene lookup at 1.0 ms — not 179 ms — because the bake step rewrites the single-row-group parquet into an indexed database. The static architecture's 158x advantage was measured against the raw parquet, not against a properly built backend. Against a built backend the gap closes to roughly parity on R1, and the backend then adds capabilities the static build has no path to.

WHAT THE BACKEND BUYS, CONCRETELY. (1) The NTScore track. 169.5 MB + 118.5 MB of HDF5 that cannot ship to a browser, served at 0.20–0.29 ms per random group read. This is the manuscript's central per-nucleotide quantity and the single most compelling thing the R1 view can show; survey [scale] listed its absence as a gap and survey [science] called it "THE headline visual asset." (2) Arbitrary boolean co-occurrence. Measured 3.4 ms for a two-cluster intersection and 28.8 ms for A ∧ B ∧ ¬C. A static build would need to precompute 900² = 810,000 pairwise intersections to answer only the two-term case, and could never answer the three-term case. (3) On-the-fly enrichment over a user-defined set, measured 13.2 ms, reproducing the published SLBP result. (4) The heavy evidence tables — 2.67 M RBP peak overlaps, 1.58 M UniProt features, 180,000 scored pairs — queryable without shipping 90 MB.

WHAT IT COSTS, AND WHY I THINK IT IS PAYABLE. A machine someone must keep alive. That is a real risk for a paper and I am not going to minimize it. The mitigation is that the same bake script emits a static export, so the deployment is deliberately three-legged: a live Cloud Run service for the full experience, an immutable Docker image on Zenodo with a DOI so anyone can `docker run` the whole portal in perpetuity, and a static GitHub Pages fallback under the lab org for the read-only paths. The paper cites all three. If the GCP project is reclaimed the DOI and the Pages URL still resolve; if GitHub changes policy the DOI and the container still work. The failure mode that kills most paper portals — one VM, one personal account, one graduating student — is engineered out rather than accepted.

OPERATIONAL COST, MEASURED NOT GUESSED. Server RSS was 62 MB after opening DuckDB, 141 MB after five full R1 requests, 161 MB after 16 concurrent cursors. A 1 vCPU / 1 GiB Cloud Run instance is generous. At min-instances=1 that is roughly $18–25/month; at min-instances=0 it is near zero but pays a 3–8 s cold start on the first click from a paper link, which is the worst possible first impression. The plan is min-instances=1 for the first 12 months post-publication and 0 thereafter, funded as a line item, with the DOI'd container as the permanent answer.

SPECIFIC DESIGN TRADEOFFS TAKEN. Frozen layout over live force — deep links and figure recognizability beat interactivity, with live force as an opt-in. SVG for the 519-node network over canvas — 2,620 edges is well within SVG, and hit-testing, focus rings and CSS hover come free; canvas is reserved for the 180,000-point UMAP where SVG is simply not an option. A typed AST over a SQL box — a SQL endpoint would be more powerful and is an injection and DoS surface I am not willing to expose publicly; the SQL preview gives transparency without the risk, and the published DuckDB file gives real SQL to anyone who wants it. JSON over binary for NTScore by default — the worst case is 13 KB gzipped, so the binary path exists only for the minimap. Region-variant cluster templates over one generic page — 600 clusters have no pLDDT and 434 have no PWM, so one template would show empty panels on most pages. Showing non-significant results — the APEX lamina q=0.725 and the four ns kinetics metrics stay on screen, because an expert reader who checks and finds them omitted will distrust everything else.

WHAT I AM DELIBERATELY NOT BUILDING IN v1. Mouse (a parallel 827,161-instance motifome exists but roughly doubles the build and has 25.3% annotation coverage against 63.9% for human). The SOX2 design story from Fig 5/6 (different audience, different data tree). Isoform selection in the generic gene search (only one transcript per gene exists; the CD47/CD44 isoform comparison ships as a fixed case-study page instead). A user-facing sequence-scan box (MIRTO motifs are attribution regions, not PWM scans, and a scan box would misrepresent the method).
risks: BLOCKING SCIENTIFIC CONFLICT, unresolved. The manuscript says 'MLXIPL ... contains the M2 utr3_0027 motifs (Fig. 4a)', but modules.json assigns utr3_0027 to M1, and the code that actually built Fig 4a (build_mlxipl_signatures.py, MLXIPL_M2_signatures.csv) uses utr3_0227, which is M2. Every data file agrees this is a one-character typo. MLXIPL is the only gene the manuscript names for M2, so the portal's M2 landing card will contradict either the paper or the data. This is a one-question email to the author and it should be sent before P2 starts. Do not resolve it silently.

I measured single-connection latency only. NO concurrency or load test was run. All quoted numbers (1.0 ms gene lookup, 28.8 ms boolean, 13.2 ms enrichment) are min-of-5 warm timings on one laptop connection. DuckDB read-only with per-request cursors should parallelize, but N simultaneous heavy scans on 1 vCPU will queue, and I have not established what N is. A k6 or locust run against the container is required in P0 before any capacity claim is made, and the min-instances / vCPU sizing above should be treated as provisional until it exists.

The 5'UTR NTScore file lives at explore_biology/01.protein_localization/analysis/data/h5cache/outputs_utr5_score_0326.h5 — an incidental location inside an unrelated analysis folder. Survey [scale] did not list it as a portal input at all; only survey [science] found it. Its 18,093 keys match the motif transcript set exactly, while the 3'UTR file has 18,585. Nothing in any documented pipeline regenerates either file. If that directory is ever cleaned up, the single most compelling feature of R1 disappears with no way to rebuild it short of rerunning MIRTO inference. Copy both into the versioned snapshot at bake time and record their provenance, and confirm with the author that no newer version exists.

There is NO per-nucleotide score for the CDS or the protein, and no delta-attention matrix anywhere on disk (Fig 3a is drawn from synthetic data, per PANELS.md). So the protein panel is permanently asymmetric with the UTR panels, and the portal can never show a reader the actual attribution that caused a stretch to be called a motif — which is the one thing that would fully answer 'why is this highlighted'. pLDDT is a genuine substitute for visual interest but it is a different quantity and must be labelled as one. Whether attention can be recomputed for a small set of featured transcripts from the MIRTO checkpoint is an open question requiring GPU inference; the surveys did not establish it.

My on-the-fly enrichment uses a TRANSCRIPT-level universe (18,006 utr3-motif transcripts) while the published cluster_term_enrichment.csv.gz uses a GENE-level universe (17,761 for utr3). My benchmark returned SLBP at k=23/n=196/fold 51.5 where the published table says k=22/n=196/fold 48.62. The numbers are close enough to validate the plumbing and far enough apart to embarrass the paper if a reader compares them without explanation. The workbench must either match the published gene-level definition exactly or name the universe on every result — I have specified the latter, but which one the author wants is not established.

The public POST /query/* endpoints are the main new attack surface and their guardrails are DESIGNED, NOT TESTED. Depth 6, 24 leaf terms, 512 MB memory limit, 5 s statement timeout, 50,000-row cap and per-IP rate limits are all reasonable numbers but none has been validated against an adversarial AST. A pathological OR-of-substring-scans query could plausibly exceed the timeout budget in a way the cost estimator does not predict. This needs a dedicated fuzzing pass in P4, and the rate limits need tuning against the load test that has not yet been run.

Hosting ownership is entirely unestablished. There is no git repo in the task directory, no CI, no stated deployment target, no GCP project, no domain, and no answer to who pays the ~$20/month or who receives the uptime alerts. My recommendation to put the repo and the Cloud Run project under a lab or institutional org rather than a personal account is the single highest-leverage decision for long-term availability, and it is a decision I cannot make. If it lands on a personal account, the URL dies when the account is renamed and the three-legged survival plan collapses to one leg.

STREME gap-fill cost is ASSUMED, not verified by me. Survey [clusters] measured 64.3 s for prot_0002 and 5-10 s for UTR clusters and extrapolated ~2.4 CPU-hours for the 387 never-run clusters. I did not re-run it. If protein clusters are slower than that sample suggests, the P2 exit criteria slip. Independently, ~100-150 protein clusters are expected to return nothing significant even after running (prot_0002 already did), so the 'every cluster gets a logo' goal is not achievable and the fallback path is load-bearing, not decorative.

203 RBP names are raw POSTAR3 labels with no alias table anywhere in the data: U2AF65/U2AF2, TDP43/TARDBP, UNR/CSDE1, IMP3/IGF2BP3, HNRNPH/HNRNPH1, plus two opaque labels ('ACI' with 4,960 entries, 'SDOS'). Any RBP facet in the workbench will double-count the same protein and split its evidence across method columns. The fix is a hand-curated ~15-row alias CSV, which is an afternoon of work but requires someone who knows the nomenclature to sign off. Until it exists, RBP-faceted counts are subtly wrong.

Cross-module edges have NO consensus pair data at all — consensus_pair_scores.csv.gz contains zero rows where the two clusters sit in different modules, so all 757 cross-module edges including the M5×M1 block the manuscript specifically discusses (192 undirected edges) fall to the tier-2 fallback. My design names the tier honestly, but the manuscript's own headline cross-module example will show a visibly weaker panel than an ordinary intra-module edge. Closing this properly means re-running 17_consensus_association.py over the 757 pairs using consensus_presence.npz; the surveys established this is feasible but nobody has measured how long it takes or whether the results would be publishable.

Coverage holes are large and will be visible everywhere: 434 of 900 clusters have no PWM, 437 have no term at FDR<0.05, 229 have neither, 387 have no module, and 9,247 of 18,093 transcripts (51.1%) belong to no module. The design specifies explicit states for all of these, but the aggregate effect is that a reader exploring at random will hit a partially-empty page more often than a full one. This is a property of the science, not the portal, and if the author expects the portal to feel uniformly rich it will not, no matter how the fallbacks are built.

Two pieces of layout and identity are generated, not loaded, and could drift from the published figures: the 519-node network coordinates (no node-level layout exists on disk; averaging the pair-UMAP does not separate M1/M2/M5/M6) and the 6x6 meta-adjacency (computed nowhere). Neither will reproduce Fig 3e pixel-for-pixel. Separately, three conflicting module color mappings exist in the codebase — I chose the four-script MCOL used in the published Fig 3d/3e/ED3b, which means the portal will NOT match the Fig 3c UMAP image if that image is embedded anywhere without recoloring.

A canonical RefSeq a reader is likely to paste can fail. I verified that TP53's transcript in this dataset is NM_001276696; a search for NM_000546, the RefSeq most people associate with TP53, resolves to nothing. Table C has no gene_symbol column, so the 1,117 motif-free transcripts cannot even be labelled with a gene name from available data. Building a decent alias/suggestion layer requires an external RefSeq→symbol map (NCBI gene2refseq or a one-off mygene lookup) that does not currently exist in the project. Without it, a legitimate identifier is indistinguishable from a typo.

The DuckDB file is 225.5 MB and the full data layer is ~515 MB baked into the container image. That is fine for Cloud Run but it makes the image slow to pull on a cold start and makes the Zenodo deposit chunky. I did not measure container cold-start time with a 515 MB image — the 3-8 s figure quoted for Cloud Run cold starts is a general expectation, not something I benchmarked here, and a large image could make it materially worse. If cold start matters, the h5 files may need to move to a mounted bucket, which reintroduces a network hop on the NTScore path I measured at 0.2 ms locally.

name: MIRTO Bilingual Motifome Portal
one_liner: A Dash (Plotly) multi-page portal over the 889,215-instance human motifome: search a transcript to read its 5'UTR/3'UTR/protein with clickable highlighted motifs on live NTScore tracks, drill any motif into its cluster's logo, enrichment and protein partners, and explore the six protein-RNA meta-modules as an interactive co-occurrence network — built entirely in pandas/Plotly with zero custom React components.
stack:
Python 3.10.13 (/opt/anaconda3/envs/bio/bin/python). **Dash 3.1.1 + Plotly 6.2.0 — both ALREADY INSTALLED and verified in the user's env**, alongside pyarrow 21.0.0, pandas 2.3.3, numpy 1.26.4, h5py 3.11.0, logomaker 0.8.7. NOT installed (verified by importlib.find_spec across all four interpreters): streamlit, panel, holoviews, bokeh, shiny, gradio, dash_cytoscape, dash_bio, duckdb, altair, datashader, fastapi.

FRAMEWORK CHOICE: **Dash**. Honest evaluation of the five candidates against the three requirements:

(1) STREAMLIT — fastest prototype, structurally wrong here. Its execution model re-runs the whole script on every interaction; 350 MB of state survives only via @st.cache_resource. The fatal issue is R1: a sequence viewer with per-motif click handling must be emitted as raw HTML through st.markdown(unsafe_allow_html=True) or components.html. The former strips event handlers; the latter is a sandboxed iframe that cannot call back into Python without writing a bidirectional custom component (React + npm build) — precisely the thing this angle exists to avoid. st.plotly_chart(on_select=...) (1.35+) does give R3 selection events, so R3 is feasible, but R1 is not without leaving Python. Eliminate.

(2) PANEL/HOLOVIEWS — the strongest runner-up and the only framework with a better answer than Dash to one sub-problem: `pn.reactive.ReactiveHTML` lets you declare arbitrary HTML with `_template` + `_scripts` and wire DOM events straight to Python parameters, which is a cleaner sequence viewer than Dash's pattern-matching callbacks. Datashader would also handle the 180k-point UMAP natively. Rejected on human factors, not capability: three overlapping APIs (Panel / HoloViews / Bokeh) the user has never touched, a Bokeh Document + Tornado runtime whose failure modes are opaque to a matplotlib user, the smallest community of the five, and it is not installed. If the user already knew hvplot this would be the pick.

(3) SHINY FOR PYTHON — excellent reactive graph (finer-grained than Dash's callback DAG), and @render.ui returns arbitrary HTML. But click-to-inspect on a Plotly figure requires shinywidgets + ipywidgets plumbing, custom DOM events need hand-written Shiny.setInputValue JS anyway, the Python port is young, and the user has no R/Shiny background to transfer. Not installed.

(4) GRADIO — built for single-model demos. No layout system for a 3-panel portal, no graph component, no route/URL story, no path to clickable sequence text. Eliminate.

(5) DASH — chosen. Six decisive properties: (a) `dcc.Graph` exposes clickData/hoverData/selectedData as ordinary Python callback Inputs, so R3's "click a node or edge, show details" is a ten-line callback with no JS; (b) **Dash components are React components rendered into the page DOM, not an iframe** — an `html.Span` per motif is real, clickable, CSS-styleable DOM reachable by pattern-matching callbacks, which makes R1's hardest requirement need ZERO custom components; (c) `dcc.Location` + `dash.register_page` give real shareable URLs (/gene/NM_001101, /cluster/utr3_0215, /pair/prot_0040/utr5_0004) — mandatory for a paper companion; (d) clientside callbacks let the two perf-critical paths drop into plain JS without abandoning the Python app; (e) `go.Scattergl` renders the 180,000-point Fig 3c UMAP in WebGL; (f) it deploys as a plain Flask/WSGI app under gunicorn. Its real weaknesses — callback-graph tangle at scale, and no built-in force layout — are both mitigated here: the former by a strict one-`dcc.Store`-per-view discipline, the latter because the survey established there are no node coordinates on disk and the layout must be frozen at build time anyway (so Plotly's lack of a force engine costs nothing).

Additional pip installs required (no build toolchain, no npm): dash-ag-grid (sortable/filterable/exportable tables), dash-bootstrap-components or pure CSS (I recommend pure CSS lifted from the user's own 03.panel_code_index.html), gunicorn. Optional: orjson (faster callback serialization). Explicitly NOT used: dash-bio (its SequenceViewer's `coverage` prop has an undocumented end-exclusivity convention that would silently collide with this dataset's 0-based-inclusive contract, and it cannot render an NTScore track), dash_cytoscape (unnecessary — coordinates are precomputed), duckdb (the in-RAM index is 0.27 ms/query, faster than DuckDB's measured 7.3 ms best case).

VERSIONS TO PIN in requirements.txt: dash==3.1.1, plotly==6.2.0, dash-ag-grid==31.3.1, pandas==2.3.3, pyarrow==21.0.0, numpy==1.26.4, h5py==3.11.0, logomaker==0.8.7, gunicorn==23.0.0.
architecture:
Let $SD = /Users/wangyanz/Desktop/Project/sequence_design (all absolute input paths below are under it).

TWO-STAGE, following the user's own documented convention ("outputs relocatable, external inputs absolute" — stated in every figure3_4 README):

  STAGE 1  code/bake.py        absolute $SD paths IN  ->  code/portal/data/ OUT   (offline, idempotent, ~6 min)
  STAGE 2  code/portal/app.py  relative data/ paths only -> Dash server           (no $SD reference anywhere)

This split means the app directory can be zipped, moved to a lab VM, or committed without a single path edit, and bake.py is the only file that ever touches the 300+ MB of source parquet/HDF5.

--- RUNTIME DATA TIERS (all latencies measured by me on this machine, not estimated) ---

TIER A — HOT, resident in the Python process at boot (measured 1.03 s boot, 203 MB):
  * motifs_slim.feather -> pandas frame, 889,215 x 10, dtypes forced to category (gene_symbol, region, motif_cluster) / int32 (motif_start, motif_end) / float32 (motif_score, motif_entropy, plddt). Measured 153.3 MB resident. Held TWICE, once .set_index('sequence_id').sort_index() for R1 and once .set_index('motif_cluster').sort_index() for R2 — total with both indexes measured 352.6 MB.
  * sequences.feather -> 19,210 x 4 (refseq_id_without_ver, utr5_sequence, utr3_sequence, protein_sequence), deduplicated with drop_duplicates('refseq_id_without_ver') (verified lossless by the survey: all 1,296 duplicate groups byte-identical). Measured 49 MB.
  * The small network layer, all as plain dicts/frames: edges (2,620 x 15), modules.json (6), consensus_meta (1,226), cluster_labels (4,096 rows), nodes+frozen xy (900), meta_edges (15), search index (76,902 tokens). Together < 15 MB.
  Measured lookup latency on these: gene/transcript lookup 0.27 ms mean, cluster lookup 0.20 ms mean.

TIER B — COLD, on disk, opened once and read lazily per request:
  * The two NTScore HDF5 files stay where they are, opened once at boot with h5py and never loaded: $SD/data/outputs_utr3_score_0318.h5 (169.5 MB, 18,585 keys) and $SD/explore_biology/01.protein_localization/analysis/data/h5cache/outputs_utr5_score_0326.h5 (118.5 MB, 18,093 keys — exactly 1:1 with the motif table). **Measured random per-transcript read: 0.379 ms mean / 1.645 ms max (utr3), 0.202 ms / 0.467 ms (utr5).** This is the single biggest architectural win of the server approach over static hosting: 288 MB of per-nucleotide score never has to be baked, downsampled, or shipped, yet it is available at sub-millisecond latency at full resolution.
  * Per-transcript annotation shards, data/ann/<refseq>.json.gz (18,093 files, ~46 MB total, median 2.4 KB). Annotations are deliberately EXCLUDED from Tier A: I measured the 11 raw annotation columns at 435.2 MB resident, more than doubling the process. Survey-measured shard read is 1.13 ms, so paying it lazily on the motif-click drawer is free.
  * Per-cluster member shards, data/cluster/<cluster>.json.gz (900 files, ~42 MB).

MEASURED END-TO-END: full R1 gene-page assembly (3 sequence slices + all motif spans + both NTScore arrays) = **0.67 ms p50 / 0.99 ms p95 / 6.43 ms max** over 80 random transcripts. With a per-request assertion that seq[start:end+1] == motifs for EVERY motif on the page it is 1.85 ms p50 — cheap enough that I recommend leaving the assertion permanently on in dev and behind a flag in prod.

--- REQUEST PATH ---

  browser URL /gene/NM_001101
    -> dcc.Location.pathname
    -> dash.register_page router picks pages/gene.py
    -> callback(Input('url','pathname')) -> dict lookup in Tier A (0.27 ms)
    -> h5py read of NTScore (0.38 ms)
    -> build (i) a plotly go.Figure for the track stack and (ii) a list of html.Span for the sequence
    -> Dash serializes the component tree to JSON -> React renders into the page DOM
  motif click
    -> pattern-matching Input({'type':'mspan','idx': ALL}, 'n_clicks')
    -> callback resolves which index changed, lazily gunzips data/ann/<refseq>.json.gz (1.13 ms)
    -> writes into dcc.Store('sel-instance') -> drawer callback renders annotation chips

--- STATE DISCIPLINE (the thing that keeps a Dash app maintainable for a non-JS author) ---
One dcc.Store per view, holding a single JSON dict that IS the view state, and one URL-sync callback per view. Every other callback reads that Store and writes DOM. This keeps the callback DAG a shallow star instead of a mesh, which is the failure mode that makes large Dash apps unmaintainable. URL is the source of truth; the Store is a cache of the parsed URL plus transient UI (open drawer, active filter chips).

--- DEPLOYMENT ---
gunicorn -w 2 --preload -b 0.0.0.0:8050 app:server. `--preload` forks after boot so the pandas categorical code arrays and numpy buffers are copy-on-write shared between workers (the backing buffers are shared even though Python refcounts are not, because our Tier A frame is deliberately all-categorical/int32/float32 with no object columns) — 2 workers cost far less than 2x352 MB. Target: a lab VM or an institutional container host with 1 GB RAM. A static export is NOT possible for this design and that is a deliberate trade (see tradeoffs).

--- WHAT MAKES THIS DEFENSIBLE ---
Every view carries the co-occurrence caveat in persistent chrome, every edge shows its four gate values inline, and the resolution selector (module / cluster / consensus) is a visible global control because the same question returns 4,348 / 49 / 15 genes at those three levels.

views.title: Landing & search
views.purpose: Give a first-time reader arriving from the paper a working entry point in one action, and make the scale and the caveat visible before anything else. Solves the 'empty search box' problem the survey flagged by seeding 22 manuscript-vetted examples.
views.layout:

Two columns: a wide reading column and a sticky right drawer. The drawer is empty (showing a hint) until a motif is clicked, then it fills without moving the sequence. views.title: Motif cluster (R2)
views.purpose: REQUIREMENT R2. For a motif: its cluster identity (logo, consensus, position), the annotations on it, and how it associates with protein features — via the cluster's gated partner clusters. Region-conditional: protein and UTR clusters get different panels rather than one template with empty slots.

Header band, then a 2-column body: left = what the cluster IS, right = what it ASSOCIATES with. views.title: How this was built, and why the top raw hits are wrong
views.purpose: Turn the project's biggest methodological caveat into its most persuasive page. Makes the delta-attention/NTScore definition, the filter funnel, and the ZNF-paralogy correction inspectable rather than asserted. Also carries the data snapshot, coverage and downloads.
views.layout:
Long-scroll, sticky pill nav, step cards in a 43/57 prose+figure grid — reusing the layout idiom the user already authored in MODULE_IDENTIFICATION_WALKTHROUGH.html.

+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| [sticky pills] 1 motifs . 2 clusters . 3 pairs . 4 paralogy . 5 modules . 6 data  |
+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| 1. WHAT IS A MOTIF HERE                                                           |
| +-------------------------+  delta-attention = observed protein-UTR attention     |
| | pipeline flow diagram   |  minus the same matrix with UTR masked. Peaks in the  |
| | seq -> MIRTO -> NTScore |  residual, intersected with high NTScore, define a    |
| |  \-> attention -> delta |  motif instance.  [!] Fig 3a is a schematic drawn     |
| +-------------------------+  from synthetic data - no attention matrices stored.  |
|                                                                                   |
| 2. FOUR NESTED OBJECTS                          instance -> unique id ->          |
|    889,215      577,186        900        513   cluster -> module                 |
|    [==========][=========][========][=======]  interactive: click any tier        |
|                                                                                   |
| 3. THE FUNNEL                                                                     |
|    180,000 scored pairs                                                           |

viz_units.name: Typeahead search

keyboard up/down/enter
paste an ENSG/ENST directly

viz_units.name: Corpus stat tiles

viz_units.name: Excluded-transcript empty state
viz_units.what_it_shows: Why a famous gene returns nothing: 1,117 transcripts have no motifs, 666 because they exceed the 7,784 nt model context.
viz_units.encoding: Card with the gene name, its measured length, the cap, and a bar showing the overrun.
viz_units.data_source: data/excluded.json baked from the set difference of GRCh37 parquet refseq_id_without_ver minus motif sequence_ids, joined to transcript_length; symbols recovered from module_gene_index.csv refseq_ids where possible
interactions: suggests the nearest motif-bearing transcript of the same gene if one exists

viz_units.name: Transcript picker
viz_units.what_it_shows: The alternative transcripts of the 215 genes (1.20%) that have more than one.
viz_units.encoding: Inline select, each option showing RefSeq + region lengths + motif count; hidden entirely for the 17,632 single-transcript genes.
viz_units.data_source: motifs_slim.feather (gene_symbol, sequence_id) + sequences.feather region lengths
interactions: select -> /gene/<other refseq>

viz_units.name: Region section header + coverage bar
viz_units.what_it_shows: Per region: length, motif count, SeqScore, and the fraction of bases covered by motifs (utr5 median 0.307, utr3 0.261, protein 0.288).
viz_units.encoding: Rule-line header with a thin coverage bar underneath; region colour (utr5 #E69F00, utr3 #A85A00, protein #0072B2).

interactions: click -> collapse/expand that region's panel

viz_units.name: 5'UTR NTScore track
viz_units.what_it_shows: The model's per-nucleotide conditional log-probability along the 5'UTR — the manuscript's central quantity, at full resolution.
viz_units.encoding: Filled area, x = position (1-based), y = NTScore (domain roughly -4.3..0, set per transcript); baseline at the region mean (SeqScore) as a dashed rule.
viz_units.data_source: $SD/explore_biology/01.protein_localization/analysis/data/h5cache/outputs_utr5_score_0326.h5, key <refseq>/score (float32, 18,093 keys, length verified == len(utr5_sequence)). Read live at 0.202 ms mean, 0.467 ms max (measured).
interactions: drag-select to zoom (relayoutData drives the sequence block)
hover -> position + score
shared x-axis with the motif ribbon
viz_units.library: Plotly go.Scatter fill='tozeroy' in a shared-x subplot

viz_units.name: 3'UTR NTScore track
viz_units.what_it_shows: Same for the 3'UTR, where the manuscript's ARE/ELAVL1 story lives.
viz_units.encoding: As VU-12; for regions over ~2,000 nt the trace is min/max-decimated to 2 px per pixel column server-side so the SVG stays under ~4,000 points while preserving peaks.
viz_units.data_source: $SD/data/outputs_utr3_score_0318.h5, key <refseq>/score (18,585 keys). Measured read 0.379 ms mean / 1.645 ms max.
interactions: as VU-12; zooming past the decimation threshold re-requests the full-resolution slice
viz_units.library: Plotly go.Scattergl for regions > 3,000 nt, go.Scatter otherwise

viz_units.name: Protein pLDDT step track
viz_units.what_it_shows: The protein panel's analogue of the NTScore track, since no per-residue score exists. Per-motif AlphaFold confidence, which separates ordered-domain motifs from IDR motifs (SOX2 HMG-box 0.980 vs its N-terminal IDR motif 0.320).
viz_units.encoding: Step/bar per motif span, y = plddt on a FIXED 0-1 domain (NOT 0-100 — measured min 0.1, median 0.8, max 1.0), with 0.5 and 0.7 reference rules; explicitly labelled 'per motif, not per residue'.
viz_units.data_source: motifs_slim.feather (region=='protein', motif_start, motif_end, plddt) — 254,466 non-null protein rows, 0 for UTR
interactions: hover -> plddt value
click -> selects the motif
viz_units.library: Plotly go.Bar with base/width from spans

viz_units.name: Motif ribbon
viz_units.what_it_shows: Every motif on the region as a positioned rectangle — a single lane, because the survey proved max stacking depth is exactly 1 across all 53,367 (transcript, region) groups.
viz_units.encoding: Rects, x0=motif_start, x1=motif_end+1, fill = module colour (grey #A7A7A7 for the 45.3% of instances in no-module clusters), opacity ~ normalised motif_score; 1px stroke so the 6.0% abutting pairs stay distinct.
viz_units.data_source: motifs_slim.feather (sequence_id, region, motif_start, motif_end, motif_cluster, motif_score) + data/cluster_module.json
interactions: click -> clickData drives the instance drawer
hover -> mini card
shared x with the score track
viz_units.library: Plotly go.Bar (horizontal, base=start) — chosen over shapes because only traces emit clickData

viz_units.name: Sequence text panel
viz_units.what_it_shows: The actual residues with motifs highlighted in place — the literal text of R1. THE central unit of the portal.
viz_units.encoding: Monospace 13px/1.75, 60 chars per line, 10-char groups. Each motif is one html.Span with background = module colour at 18% alpha, a 1px inset outline in the region colour, and id={'type':'mspan','idx':raw_motif_index}. Unhighlighted runs are plain text nodes. Rendered as a flat run-length alternation of gap-text and motif-spans — measured p50 89 / p99 279 / max 381 elements for all three regions on one page, which is trivial for React.
viz_units.data_source: sequences.feather (utr5_sequence, utr3_sequence, protein_sequence) sliced with the verified contract seq[motif_start:motif_end+1] (100.000000% exact over all 889,215 rows); motifs_slim for spans
interactions: click a span -> pattern-matching callback fills the drawer
hover -> tooltip
text is selectable and copy-pasteable (a hard requirement for wet-lab users, and the reason this is DOM and not canvas)
filter chips dim non-matching spans to 25% opacity without reflowing
viz_units.library: Pure dash.html.Span + CSS. NO custom React component, NO dash-bio, NO canvas.

viz_units.name: Coordinate gutter
viz_units.what_it_shows: 1-based sequence coordinates at the start of each 60-char line.
viz_units.encoding: Right-aligned mono numerals in a 56px gutter, muted colour.
viz_units.data_source: derived from sequence length
interactions: click a number -> copies that coordinate

viz_units.name: RNA/DNA alphabet toggle
viz_units.what_it_shows: UTR sequences and motif strings as RNA (U) — matching the manuscript's UCAUC/UCUCC/GCCACC — or as the stored DNA alphabet.
viz_units.encoding: Two-state segmented control; RNA is the default because the paper is written in RNA.
viz_units.data_source: storage is DNA-only (verified: utr5/utr3 alphabets are A/C/G/T with zero U); transliteration is display-only and NEVER applied to protein, where U is selenocysteine
interactions: toggle re-renders sequence spans and motif strings; search accepts both and normalises to T before matching

viz_units.name: Motif hover tooltip
viz_units.what_it_shows: A four-line mini-card without a click: coordinates, cluster + module, score, and the single top annotation.
viz_units.encoding: Dark card, 260px, arrow anchored to the span; includes a 40px-wide inline mini score bar.
viz_units.data_source: motifs_slim + the already-loaded per-transcript annotation shard
interactions: hover, 120 ms delay, dismisses on leave
viz_units.library: dcc.Tooltip for the ribbon; CSS ::after for the DOM spans (avoids 381 Tooltip components)

viz_units.data_source: data/ann/<refseq>.json.gz (lazily gunzipped, 1.13 ms measured) built from motif_full_annotations.parquet with the region mask applied
interactions: opens on span or ribbon click
'open cluster' link
'copy coordinates' and 'copy sequence' buttons

viz_units.name: Annotation chip rows
viz_units.what_it_shows: Per-instance annotations grouped by database, each chip carrying its source, its overlap rule, and a deep link.
viz_units.encoding: One row per database with the display name from the coverage JSON; chips coloured by layer (RNA #2E7D9A vs protein #9C6B1E); a greyed 'none' chip rather than a hidden row when a database is empty.

InterPro/UniProt/ELM chips built from ID-bearing re-joins, never by comma-splitting (wrong for 41.34% / 6.894% of rows respectively).

click -> interpro.ebi.ac.uk / uniprot.org / elm.eu.org

viz_units.name: RBP method-agreement badge
viz_units.what_it_shows: How many of the four CLIP methods support this motif's RBP evidence (measured distribution over 634,749 UTR motifs: 0 methods 308,753 / 1 144,288 / 2 95,096 / 3 57,474 / 4 29,138) — a free, honest confidence axis.
viz_units.encoding: Four small squares [e][P][i][C], filled if that method contributed; caption '3 of 4 methods'.

interactions: hover -> which RBPs came from which method, with the alias note (U2AF65=U2AF2, TDP43=TARDBP, UNR=CSDE1, IMP3=IGF2BP3, HNRNPH=HNRNPH1)

viz_units.name: Gene module fingerprint bar
viz_units.what_it_shows: Which of the six modules this transcript's motif clusters belong to, and how many instances have no module at all.

interactions: click a segment -> filters the sequence view to that module
click -> /module/M<n>

row click -> selects the motif and scrolls the sequence
CSV export of the visible rows

interactions: none

viz_units.name: Requirement cards

viz_units.data_source: static
interactions: click -> the view, seeded with an example

viz_units.name: Three-tier cluster name
viz_units.what_it_shows: A human-readable name for every one of the 900 clusters, never a bare id.
viz_units.encoding: Name plus a small tier badge: tier 1 curated (37 clusters), tier 2 top FDR<0.05 term (463), tier 3 synthesised from consensus + composition + size (437, almost all UTR).

interactions: hover the tier badge -> where the name came from

viz_units.name: Sequence logo
viz_units.what_it_shows: The cluster's information-content logo from its real STREME PWM.
viz_units.encoding: Per-position stacked letters, height = information content in bits; nucleotides A #009E73 / C #0072B2 / G #E69F00 / U #D55E00; amino acids by the examples_lib.aacol scheme (L #C1121F, hydrophobic #E8862E, polar #2A9D8F, charged #3557A6).
viz_units.data_source: $SD/manuscript/main_figures_code/figure3_4/motif_pair_network/intermediate/consensus_repertoire.pkl -> per cluster motifs[].pwm (w x 20 protein, w x 4 RNA), nsites, evalue, consensus, coverage. Covers 451 of 900 clusters; baked to a 0.56 MB JSON.
interactions: hover a column -> the four/twenty letter probabilities
toggle between the cluster's multiple consensus (median 2, max 10)
viz_units.library: Plotly go.Scatter mode='text' with per-letter textfont.size scaled to bits — chosen over a logomaker PNG because it stays interactive, themeable and vector; logomaker+SVG data-URI kept as a fallback for print export

viz_units.name: Logo provenance badge
viz_units.what_it_shows: Whether the logo is a real STREME fit or a derived fallback — non-negotiable, since a PWM logo reads as 'the site' and coverage can be as low as 0.212.
viz_units.encoding: Badge reading 'STREME E=9.2e-14, 394 sites, coverage 0.51' or 'derived from member instances - not a STREME motif'.
viz_units.data_source: consensus_repertoire.pkl (n_sig, evalue, nsites) and consensus_meta.csv (coverage, carriers)
interactions: hover -> what coverage means (fraction of cluster members the consensus matches at >=0.5 bits/pos)

viz_units.name: Positional histogram
viz_units.what_it_shows: Where along the region this cluster's motifs fall, 5'->3' or N->C — the evidence behind 'cap-proximal' (utr5_0079) and 'concentrated at the start codon' (utr5_0090, median_pos 0.791).
viz_units.encoding: 20-bin bar sparkline with a median tick; x labelled 5' and 3' (or N and C).
viz_units.data_source: computed at bake for ALL 900 clusters as relpos=(motif_start+motif_end)/2/region_length, joining motif_full_annotations to sequences.feather (verified 18,093/18,093 join, 0 out-of-range); validated against the 142 published pos_hist entries in streme_pos_cache_all6.pkl (e.g. utr3_0215 median_pos 0.4441, n=566)
interactions: hover a bin -> count and position range

viz_units.name: Consensus repertoire table
viz_units.what_it_shows: All 1-10 consensus strings of the cluster with their honesty metrics.
viz_units.encoding: Table: cid, consensus (mono, RNA alphabet), coverage as an inline bar, carriers as a count.
viz_units.data_source: consensus_meta.csv (cid, cluster, module, region, consensus, coverage, carriers) — 1,226 rows over 451 clusters
interactions: click a row -> the logo above switches to that consensus

data_pipeline:
ONE script, `code/bake.py`, run with /opt/anaconda3/envs/bio/bin/python. It is the ONLY file that references $SD = /Users/wangyanz/Desktop/Project/sequence_design. Idempotent, ~6 min, writes `code/portal/data/`. STEP 0 — ASSERT BEFORE BUILDING (fail loudly on a data refresh) * Port $SD/../scratchpad/r1/s05_full.py: assert seq[motif_start:motif_end+1] == motifs for all 889,215 rows. Verified 100.000000%. * Assert (motif_end - motif_start + 1) == motif_length for all rows. * Port s18_verify_filter.py: recompute all 8 published annotation coverage percentages under the `applies` mask and assert exact agreement with annotation_coverage_stats.json. * Assert motif_cluster == f'{prefix}_{kmeans_label:04d}' (0 mismatches). * Assert the sequence table dedup is lossless (1,296 duplicate groups, all byte-identical). STEP 1 — CORE FRAMES (Tier A, loaded into RAM at app boot) IN $SD/sequence_annotation/sequence_annotation_human/data/processed/motif_full_annotations.parquet (44.5 MB, 889,215 x 24) OUT data/motifs_slim.feather — 10 cols (gene_symbol, sequence_id, region, motif_start, motif_end, motifs, motif_cluster, motif_score, motif_entropy, plddt) with dtypes forced to category/int32/float32. **Measured 153.3 MB resident, 0.31 s to read.** IN $SD/data/GRCh37_latest_rna_sequence_pairs_long_transcript.parquet OUT data/sequences.feather — drop_duplicates('refseq_id_without_ver') -> 19,210 rows x 4. Join key is refseq_id_without_ver (100% coverage of the 18,093 motif transcripts; the 'RefSeq mRNA ID' column would silently drop 1,617 genes). Combined measured boot: **1.03 s, 202.7 MB.** STEP 2 — ANNOTATION SHARDS (Tier B, on disk) Adapt the survey's working builder (scratchpad/r1/s13_fullbuild.py, 18 s for all 18,093 shards) with TWO REQUIRED FIXES: (a) apply the region mask from annotation_coverage_stats.json's `applies` field, dropping MobiDB/IDPO/SignalP from UTR rows — this removes 212,449 spurious protein-disorder annotations that would otherwise tell an RNA biologist that 67% of 5'UTR motifs have intrinsic disorder; (b) replace the comma-joined string columns with ID-bearing re-joins on raw_motif_index — interpro from processed/01.interpro/motif_interpro_annotations.parquet (overlapping_interpro_labels) + interpro_entry_map.csv, uniprot recomputed from processed/03.uniprot/uniprot_annotation.parquet keeping type+coords, elm from raw_annotations/02.elm/elm_instances.tsv keeping ELMIdentifier, idpo_ids from processed/05.idpo. Comma-splitting is wrong for 41.34% of InterPro and 6.894% of UniProt rows and shreds ELM names outright. OUT data/ann/.json.gz — 18,093 files, ~46 MB total, median 2.4 KB, max 11.3 KB. Measured read 1.13 ms. STEP 3 — CLUSTER LAYER (900 clusters) OUT data/clusters.json — 900 rows: cluster, region, module|null, n_instances (min 218 / median 920 / max 5,755), n_genes, n_transcripts, three-tier display name, has_logo, has_sig_term, n_partners_strict, n_partners_relaxed, top_term. ~200 KB. OUT data/pwm.json — from consensus_repertoire.pkl, PWMs rounded to 4 dp, 451 clusters / 1,226 motifs / 56,808 cells. Measured 0.56 MB. OUT data/consensus.json — consensus_meta.csv verbatim (1,226 rows), 18 KB gz. OUT data/enrichment.json — cluster_term_enrichment.csv.gz filtered to fdr_cluster<0.05, de-duplicated on (cluster, source, display) keeping min fdr_cluster (necessary: 17,056 (cluster, display) groups are duplicated by MobiDB provenance keys — prot_0072's top 3 are otherwise all 'phase separation (curated)'), capped at 12 per cluster. **I measured this at 4,096 rows / 1.274 MB JSON / 0.226 MB gzipped, covering all 463 clusters with a significant term.** The full unfiltered table is also written per-cluster into data/cluster/.json.gz so the non-significant fallback panel has data. OUT data/poshist.json — 20-bin relative-position histogram for ALL 900 clusters (the on-disk cache covers only 142), computed as relpos=(start+end)/2/region_length. ~84 KB. Validated against the 142 published pos_hist arrays before shipping. OUT data/cluster/.json.gz — 900 member-instance shards, ~42 MB. STEP 4 — NETWORK LAYER OUT data/edges.json — phylo_corrected_candidates.csv (2,620 x 15) plus mp/mu module ids and the UMAP xy joined from cca_winner_umap.npy. ~89 KB gz. OUT data/edges_relaxed.json — protein_utr_FINAL_scores.csv filtered to passes_phylo_filter OR npmi_mip_APC>0.1 -> 7,210 rows, 9 columns. ~0.74 MB. OUT data/nodes.json — 513 module clusters from consensus_scope_clusters.csv + 6 unassigned endpoints, with **FROZEN x/y** from a single seeded igraph/networkx force layout with per-module attractors and a protein-left/UTR-right constraint, module block order from node_select.order_modules(). This file does not exist upstream and must be built; without it the graph re-settles differently on every page load and deep links become meaningless. OUT data/meta_edges.json — the 6x6 cross-module adjacency, also not on disk upstream: M1-M2 244, M1-M5 192, M2-M3 167, M1-M6 32, M1-M3 30, M2-M5 28, M3-M4 22, M5-M6 15, M3-M6 6, M2-M4 5, M2-M6 5, M3-M5 5, M4-M5 4, M1-M4 1, M4-M6 1. ~2 KB. OUT data/consensus_pairs.json — consensus_pair_scores.csv.gz filtered to cl_passes, top 3 per (p_cluster, u_cluster) -> 3,599 rows, ~703 KB. OUT data/carriers/

x.json — precomputed bitwise AND of consensus_presence.npz Pc and Uc columns for the displayed edges, so no numpy runs per request. OUT data/umap.bin — 180,000 xy quantized to uint16 (max error 0.000234 data units) + uint16 npmi + uint8 module channels. Measured 0.994 MB gzipped, versus 4.878 MB as JSON records. STEP 5 — MODULE, VALIDATION, SEARCH, THEME OUT data/modules.json (verbatim, 10 KB), data/module_go.json (module_GO_enrichment.csv, 6,389 rows, 203 KB gz), data/go_specificity.json (42 rows, 2.5 KB), data/module_genes.json (module_gene_index.csv minus the trusted_terms text column, ~512 KB), data/validation/*.json (the 8 small validation CSVs), data/theme.json (manuscript_style.PALETTE + the four-script MCOL module mapping), data/search_index.json (17,847 symbols + 18,093 RefSeq + 20,481 ENSG + 20,481 ENST; measured 1.71 MB raw / 0.42 MB gz), data/availability.json, data/excluded.json. STEP 6 — MANIFEST OUT data/manifest.json — for every input: absolute source path, size, mtime, SHA-256; plus snapshot version, build timestamp, layout seed, and the pinned package versions. Special attention to cca_winner_umap.npy, which lives in the v3 analysis tree that nothing else in the portal references. OPTIONAL PRE-STEP (recommended, ~15 min at WORKERS=10): run STREME on the 387 never-run clusters using windows_fasta()/run_streme() from 16_consensus_repertoire.py verbatim (streme --p --n $SD/data/background_sequences/background_sequences_{protein,utr3,utr5}.fasta --oc

--nmotifs 12, plus --protein --minw 6 --maxw 15 or --rna --minw 5 --maxw 12), binary at /Users/wangyanz/software/meme/bin/streme. Measured cost 64.3 s per protein cluster, 5-10 s per UTR cluster. This lifts logo coverage from 466/900 toward ~700/900 and should be done BEFORE the cluster page is designed, not retrofitted. TOTAL BAKED OUTPUT: ~92 MB on disk (46 MB annotation shards + 42 MB cluster shards + ~4 MB everything else). The two NTScore HDF5 files (288 MB) are NOT baked, NOT copied and NOT downsampled — the server reads them in place at 0.2-0.4 ms.

tradeoffs:
**Dash over Streamlit** — the honest cost is 2-3x more code for the same page. Streamlit's `st.dataframe` and implicit rerun model would have this at a demo in three days. I am paying that cost for one thing: Dash renders `html.Span` into the page DOM, reachable by a Python callback, while Streamlit's only route to custom HTML is an iframe that cannot call back without a React build step. R1's core requirement — click a highlighted motif in the sequence and inspect it — is the whole project, and it is exactly where Streamlit's abstraction breaks. If the requirement were "show a table of motifs" I would have picked Streamlit.

**Dash over Panel** — this is the closest call and I want to be plain that it is a human-factors decision, not a capability one. Panel's `ReactiveHTML` is a genuinely better sequence viewer primitive than Dash's pattern-matching callbacks, and Datashader would handle the 180k UMAP more gracefully than Scattergl. I chose Dash because it is already installed alongside Plotly 6.2.0 in the user's working env, because the user has already written 1,385 lines of Plotly graph code implementing this exact interaction contract, and because Panel's three-layer API and Bokeh runtime would put the author in unfamiliar debugging territory for the parts most likely to break. If the user ever hires a Panel-fluent collaborator, revisit.

**A server at all, versus fully-static shards** — the parallel surveys correctly concluded that a static site wins on cost, longevity and cold start. I am consciously choosing the opposite because this angle optimizes for the AUTHOR's ability to build and extend, and because a Python process buys three concrete things that static hosting cannot: (a) the 288 MB of per-nucleotide NTScore stays on the server and is read at 0.2-0.4 ms, so R1's most compelling visual needs no baking, no downsampling and no 46 MB of extra payload; (b) arbitrary cross-filtering (faceted browse, resolution switching, member-grid pagination over a 5,755-row cluster) is a pandas expression rather than a client-side index the author would have to design; (c) a change to a chart is one Python edit and a reload, not a rebuild. The price is real and I will not soften it: someone must run and patch a process, a free tier that sleeps gives a 30 s cold start on a link printed in a paper, and if the VM is reclaimed when the first author leaves, the citation dies. **Mitigation, and I would make it a release requirement: bake.py's output is a complete, self-describing static data tree, so a static fallback front-end can always be built from the same artifacts, and the Zenodo deposit of data/ preserves the science even if the server does not survive.**

**In-RAM index over DuckDB** — I measured the slim frame at 0.27 ms per gene lookup against DuckDB's best measured case of 7.3 ms on a re-partitioned parquet, with no new dependency and no file rewriting. DuckDB earns its place only if arbitrary user SQL is ever a requirement, which none of R1/R2/R3 asks for.

**Annotations on disk, not in RAM** — I measured the 11 raw annotation columns at 435.2 MB resident, which would triple the process for data needed only when a drawer opens. Paying 1.13 ms per shard read is obviously right. The cost is that a global "find every motif annotated with ELAVL1" query is not possible without a separate inverted index; I have deliberately not built one, and if that query is wanted the faceted browse view would need an extra bake artifact.

**DOM spans over canvas for the sequence** — canvas would render a 7,601 nt region faster, but the text would not be selectable or copy-pasteable, which is the first thing a wet-lab reader does. The survey's segment-count measurement (p50 89, max 381 elements) makes the DOM approach comfortably safe, so there is no real tension here — but it does mean the sequence panel cannot scale to a whole chromosome, which this project never needs.

**Plotly logos over logomaker images** — building the logo as scaled text glyphs in Plotly costs more code than calling logomaker and embedding a PNG, and it will not look quite as polished as the published figures. It buys hover, theming, vector export and dark-mode correctness across ~700 cluster pages. I keep logomaker+SVG as the print-export path so the manuscript figures and the portal can still agree exactly.

**Cross-module edges on by default** — this makes the network visibly messier than published Fig 3e. I consider hiding 28.9% of the result the worse sin, particularly since the manuscript itself discusses the M1<->M5 link. The published 52-node preset exists precisely so a reader can get the clean figure back in one click.

**Showing non-significant results** — the validation panels will look weaker than the manuscript's prose in two specific places (APEX lamina q=0.725, OMM q=0.551, and four of seven M5 metrics). This is deliberate. An expert reader checks, and a portal that only shows supporting statistics loses more credibility than the ns rows cost.

**Human-only v1** — a parallel 827,161-instance mouse motifome exists, but its annotation coverage is 25.3% versus 63.9% and it roughly doubles the build. The schema is kept species-keyed (as annotation_coverage_stats.json already is) so mouse can be added by repointing bake.py, but shipping it in v1 would halve the polish of the human portal for a feature nobody asked for.
risks: MANUSCRIPT-vs-DATA CONFLICT, BLOCKING: the manuscript's only named M2 example says 'MLXIPL ... contains the M2 utr3_0027 motifs', but modules.json assigns utr3_0027 to module 1, while the code that actually produced that figure (build_mlxipl_signatures.py, MLXIPL_M2_signatures.csv) uses utr3_0227, which is module 2. All evidence points to a one-character typo, but the portal will publicly expose the inconsistency on its M2 card whichever way it is built. This is a one-question email to the author and it should be sent before P2 starts.

SILENT MIS-SLICING ON MULTI-TRANSCRIPT GENES - I hit this myself while measuring. Keying the R1 page on gene_symbol and taking sequence_id.iloc[0] raised an assertion failure on APEX1: its two transcripts have 5'UTRs of 232 nt (NM_001244249) and 237 nt (NM_001641), so motif coordinates from one silently address the other. This affects the 215 genes (1.20%) with more than one transcript, up to 7 for BAG6. The page MUST be keyed on sequence_id and the per-request coordinate assertion must stay on in dev. The surveys reported the 100% coordinate contract correctly; the trap is in the join, not the coordinates.

The 900-cluster page quality is capped by coverage gaps the surveys measured and I have not closed: 434 of 900 clusters have no STREME PWM, 437 have no term at FDR<0.05, and 229 have NEITHER. The three-tier naming and the member-string fallback keep every page from being blank, but roughly a quarter of cluster pages will be thin. The 387-cluster STREME rerun (~15 min at WORKERS=10) is the single highest-value mitigation and should happen before P2, not after.

NETWORK LAYOUT IS NOT DERIVABLE FROM ANYTHING ON DISK. There are no node-level coordinates anywhere, and the surveys established that averaging the pair-level UMAP does not separate M1/M2/M5/M6 (centroid gaps smaller than within-module spread). A layout must be invented at bake time. Whatever it looks like, it will NOT reproduce published Fig 3e, whose placement comes from a min-linear-arrangement inside 24_bipartite_pruned_ordered.py. Readers arriving from the paper may not recognise the graph; the 52-node published preset partly mitigates this but does not reproduce the exact figure.

Plotly has no force-directed layout and no edge-bundling, so the 519-node / 2,620-edge graph will be visually denser than a d3-force or Cytoscape rendering with live physics. Node dragging is also not supported by dcc.Graph without custom relayout handling. This is a real aesthetic and ergonomic cost of the framework choice; dash_cytoscape would fix it but is not installed and would add a component whose click semantics differ from the rest of the app.

I did NOT measure the network view's browser-side render time, only the data sizes and the server-side lookups. 2,620 edges as SVG line segments plus 519 Scattergl nodes should be comfortable, but Plotly's SVG edge trace could stutter on a low-end laptop during the threshold slider drag. The clientside-callback mitigation is designed in, but the frame rate is unverified and P3's exit criterion should be measured on real hardware, not assumed.

MEMORY UNDER MULTIPLE GUNICORN WORKERS IS UNVERIFIED. I measured 202.7 MB for one process with the transcript index and 352.6 MB with both indexes. I have NOT measured how much survives copy-on-write across forked workers. The design deliberately uses all-categorical/int32/float32 columns so the numpy backing buffers should be shared, but Python refcount churn on the category objects will dirty some pages. Budget for the worst case (2 workers x 353 MB = 706 MB) until measured.

The 3'UTR NTScore decimation strategy is designed but unmeasured. Regions up to 7,601 nt need min/max decimation to stay under a few thousand SVG points, and re-requesting full resolution on zoom adds a round-trip. I verified the h5 read is 0.379 ms but not the end-to-end zoom interaction latency.

PER-NUCLEOTIDE SCORES EXIST ONLY FOR UTRs. There is no NTScore for the CDS or the protein, so the protein panel is structurally asymmetric with the two UTR panels. pLDDT is a real and discriminating substitute (cluster medians span 0.215-0.972) but it is per-motif, not per-residue, and it measures structural confidence, not model likelihood. The two must never be presented on a shared axis or in the same visual idiom.

No delta-attention matrices are stored anywhere, and PANELS.md states Fig 3a is drawn from synthetic data. The portal therefore cannot show a reader the actual attribution that defined a motif - the single most explanatory thing it could offer. Regenerating it would need GPU inference from the MIRTO checkpoint, which is out of scope. The methods page must label the schematic as illustrative.

One transcript per gene means the CD47/CD44 long-vs-short 3'UTR isoform argument - which the manuscript makes in Fig 2g - cannot be reproduced through generic search. The five-gene isoform bundle (all_utr3_scores.npz with LU/SU tracks, ELAVL1_binding_regions.parquet) exists and could become a fixed case-study page, but a generic isoform selector cannot be built and should not be implied by the UI.

The RBP facet will double-count without an alias map that does not exist: 203 POSTAR3 names with U2AF65/U2AF2, TDP43/TARDBP, UNR/CSDE1, IMP3/IGF2BP3, HNRNPH/HNRNPH1 all unreconciled, plus two opaque labels ('ACI', 4,960 entries, and 'SDOS'). Hand-curating ~15 rows is an afternoon, but it has not been done and until it is, any per-RBP count in the portal is slightly wrong.

External validation panels are gene-panel-limited (RIBOmap ~982 genes, TimeLapse-seq 206, APEX partition n=26/87/6) against an 18,093-transcript corpus, so almost every gene a visitor searches will have no functional readout. Presenting these as module-level evidence pages with denominators printed is the mitigation, but the panels will still feel like cherry-picks to a sceptical reader and no amount of design fixes that.

Fig 4b's published group sizes (n=667 vs n=460) could not be reproduced from the tf_modules intermediates, which contain 858 TFs split 447/411. If the portal renders that comparison it may print different n than the paper. Ask the author for the exact partition before printing any n, or present m1_m2_rbp_enrichment.csv's per-RBP rates and cite the figure instead of re-deriving.

No cross-reference exists from the 1,226 discovered consensus strings to any known RBP motif database (CISBP-RNA, RBPmap, ATtRACT, Ray et al.) anywhere in the trees surveyed. The portal therefore cannot answer the first question a reader will ask of UCUCC - 'is that actually the PTBP motif?' The manuscript's own SRSF3/4 and PTBP attributions are literature inferences with no enrichment row in the data, and the UI must badge them as such. TOMTOM ships with the same MEME install and could close this later.

The three conflicting module colour mappings in the user's own tree (the four-script MCOL, the CATEGORICAL cycle in motif_umap/make_individual_figures.py, and the unimplemented proposal in _shared/COLOR_TABLE.md) mean any embedded figure image may not match the portal's live colours. I have specified MCOL as canonical, but if Fig 3c's UMAP PNG is ever embedded it will disagree unless recoloured at bake time.

Deployment target is still unstated. The whole architecture assumes a process can be run somewhere with ~1 GB RAM and access to the two HDF5 files. If the answer turns out to be 'GitHub Pages only', the NTScore tracks must be baked and downsampled and this design needs its Tier B rethought - which would take P1 back several days.

The effort estimate of 24 days assumes the author is fluent in pandas/matplotlib and learning Dash as they go. The sequence viewer (VU-16) and the network graph (VU-71) are the two units where a non-JS developer is most likely to lose days to unfamiliar debugging - pattern-matching callback semantics and Plotly trace/click plumbing respectively. If either stalls, cut the browse view (P4) and the validation panels (P5) first; R1/R2/R3 are intact without them.
